questiontext.text:
Which statement DOES NOT represent a disadvantage of using the mean?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]][[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked solution

[[ if test="member(1, ta_index)" ]]

The desired algebraic property, refers to a specific property that is not possessed by the mean, and it's known as "linearity." The mean does not satisfy the property of linearity when applied to the sum or difference of random variables or datasets. This means that the mean of the sum (or difference) of two datasets is not generally equal to the sum (or difference) of the means of those datasets. To illustrate this, let's consider two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), and their respective means, denoted as \(E(X)\) and \(E(Y)\). The expected value (mean) of the sum of these two random variables is not necessarily equal to the sum of their means: \(E(X + Y) ≠ E(X) + E(Y)\)

[[/ if ]] [[ if test="member(2, ta_index)" ]]

It cannot be computed for grouped data in the cases of open classes because computing the mean (average) in grouped data with open-ended class intervals can be challenging due to the lack of specific data points within those intervals. This is because the mean relies on knowing the individual data points, and when you have open-ended intervals, you don't have access to those specific values

[[/ if ]] [[ if test="member(3, ta_index)" ]]

"it is least affected by fluctuations of the sample" is not accurate when referring to the mean. In fact, the mean is quite sensitive to fluctuations in a sample. If you want a measure that is less influenced by fluctuations or outliers, it's better to consider the median or the mode.

[[/ if ]]
